title: How to attach beads in cross-stitch
subtitle: Securing seed beads to Aida with a half cross-stitch
excerpt: Beads are attached to a cross-stitch piece by passing a threaded needle through the bead and then down through the fabric in the same motion as a half cross-stitch. The bead sits over one Aida square and is held in place by the thread running diagonally beneath it.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Modern cross-stitch bead attachment conventions follow standard seed-bead embroidery practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: A glass or plastic seed bead attached to the fabric over one Aida square using a half cross-stitch in a matching or contrasting thread. Adds texture and shine to a design.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.
Only the first diagonal of a full cross. Lighter coverage on the fabric, usually used for backgrounds or shading where the chart calls for a half-tone.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

content.text: A
bead
sits over one square of
Aida
and is held in place by a
half cross-stitch

running diagonally beneath it. Coming up through the bottom-left hole, the thread passes through the bead, then down through the top-right hole, so the bead is pinned flat against the fabric at the same angle as the lower diagonal of a full cross.
The bead takes up the same area as a standard full cross but adds a small raised point of glass or plastic. The usual choice for cross-stitch is a 11/0 seed bead, which fits comfortably over 14-count
Aida
squares. On 18-count or above, a smaller 15/0 seed bead keeps a better proportion.
What you need

items.name: Seed beads
items.substitutions: Glass beads are the standard; plastic beads are lighter but show seams

items.name: Beading thread or single-strand floss
items.qty: One strand in a matching colour
items.substitutions: A specialist beading thread (Nymo) grips beads more securely than floss on large pieces

items.name: Beading needle or fine sharp needle
items.substitutions: A standard tapestry needle is too blunt for most bead holes; use a sharp size 10 beading needle

content.text: How to attach a bead
Come up through the bottom-left hole of the square where the bead will sit.
Thread the bead onto the needle. Slide it down onto the
floss
so it rests flat on the fabric surface.
Insert the needle down through the top-right hole of the same square, moving diagonally as for a half cross-stitch.
Pull through with light tension until the bead lies flat across the square. The bead should not twist sideways; if it does, the thread is pulling from the wrong angle.

For extra security, particularly on pieces that will be handled, come back up through the bottom-left hole and through the bead again before taking the thread back down. This double-passes the thread through the bead and reduces the chance of the bead slipping.

items.symptom: The bead sits at an angle rather than lying flat
items.cause: The thread exits the fabric at the wrong point, or the bead size is too large for the fabric count.
items.fix: Check that the entry and exit holes are directly diagonal from each other (bottom-left to top-right of the same square). If the bead is still too large, try one size smaller.

items.symptom: The bead wobbles or shifts when the fabric is moved
items.cause: The thread passes through the bead only once, with insufficient tension.
items.fix: Pass the thread through the bead twice for a more secure attachment. Specialist beading thread also grips the bead hole more tightly than floss.

content.text: What to try next
Beads work well in small clusters on florals projects, replacing a group of
French knots
where a harder, more reflective texture suits the design. Try attaching a line of beads in place of back-stitch on the main stem of a botanicals piece.
